questions.sec: LI-RADS and the Common Liver Tumours
questions.q: The investigation of choice for liver tumours, on which LI-RADS is based, is:
questions.exp: The investigation of choice is triple phase CT and LI-RADS scoring is based on it. (Book p253)

questions.sec: LI-RADS and the Common Liver Tumours
questions.q: LI-RADS scoring is applied to:
questions.exp: LI-RADS scoring is done for all liver tumours. (Book p253)

questions.sec: LI-RADS and the Common Liver Tumours
questions.q: An LR-1 lesion is:
questions.exp: LR-1: 100% benign. (Book p253)

questions.sec: LI-RADS and the Common Liver Tumours
questions.q: An LR-2 lesion is:
questions.exp: LR-2: probably benign (follow up done). (Book p253)

questions.sec: LI-RADS and the Common Liver Tumours
questions.q: An LR-3 lesion indicates:
opts: Intermediate probability for HCC — follow up or biopsy
questions.exp: LR-3: intermediate probability for HCC (follow up/biopsy). (Book p253)

questions.sec: LI-RADS and the Common Liver Tumours
questions.q: LR-4 means:
questions.exp: LR-4: probably HCC. (Book p253)

questions.sec: LI-RADS and the Common Liver Tumours
questions.q: LR-5 means:
questions.exp: LR-5: 100% definite HCC. (Book p253)

questions.sec: LI-RADS and the Common Liver Tumours
questions.q: The most common benign tumour of the liver is:
questions.exp: One liners: m/c benign tumor — haemangioma. (Book p253)

questions.sec: LI-RADS and the Common Liver Tumours
questions.q: The second most common benign tumour of the liver is:
questions.exp: The one-liners list FNH (focal nodular hyperplasia) as the second m/c benign tumour. (Book p253)

questions.sec: LI-RADS and the Common Liver Tumours
questions.q: The most common malignant tumour of the liver is:
questions.exp: m/c malignant tumor: metastasis / secondaries to liver (HCC is the m/c PRIMARY malignant tumour). (Book p253)

questions.sec: LI-RADS and the Common Liver Tumours
questions.q: The most common primary malignant tumour of the liver is:
questions.exp: m/c primary malignant tumor: hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). (Book p253)

questions.q: A liver haemangioma is:
questions.exp: Liver haemangiomas are a collection of blood vessels. (Book p253)

questions.q: Liver haemangiomas are more common in:
questions.exp: Clinical features: female > male. (Book p253)

questions.q: Most liver haemangiomas are:
questions.exp: Commonly asymptomatic → incidental diagnosis. (Book p253)

questions.q: Kasabach-Merritt syndrome (consumption coagulopathy) is a complication of:
questions.exp: In very large haemangiomas: Kasabach-Merritt syndrome — consumption coagulopathy. (Book p253)

questions.q: Large haemangiomas may present with:
questions.exp: Large haemangiomas → bleeding + pain. (Book p253)

questions.q: On a non-contrast triple phase CT a haemangioma is:
questions.exp: Non-contrast phase: hypodense. (Book p253)

questions.q: The characteristic arterial phase appearance of a hepatic haemangioma is:
questions.exp: Arterial phase: peripheral nodular enhancement. (Book p253)

questions.q: An asymptomatic hepatic haemangioma is managed by:
questions.exp: Asymptomatic: conservative management. (Book p254)

questions.q: A large symptomatic haemangioma is treated by:
questions.exp: Large + symptomatic: angioembolisation. (Book p254)

questions.q: FNH is more common in:
questions.exp: FNH: female > male. (Book p254)

questions.q: FNH is usually:
questions.exp: FNH clinical features: female > male, asymptomatic, incidental diagnosis. (Book p254)

questions.q: The imaging hallmark of FNH on triple phase CT is:
questions.exp: Central stellate scar: a dilated arteriole with branches. (Book p254)

questions.q: The central stellate scar of FNH is also a feature of which renal tumour?
questions.exp: The page notes the central stellate scar is also seen in oncocytoma of the kidney. (Book p254)

questions.q: On histopathology FNH contains hepatocytes and:
opts: Atypical bile duct structures with Kupffer cells
Sheets of hepatocytes with no bile ducts
questions.exp: HPE of FNH: hepatocytes, atypical bile duct structures and Kupffer cells. (Book p254)

questions.q: Because FNH contains Kupffer cells and is usually unencapsulated it:
opts: Shows a 'hot-spot' on a sulphur colloid scan
Shows no uptake on a sulphur colloid scan
Is always hot on a PET scan
questions.exp: Kupffer cells (and the usually unencapsulated nature) → 'hot-spot' on a sulphur colloid scan. (Book p254)

questions.q: Alpha-fetoprotein in FNH is:
questions.exp: α-fetoprotein (AFP) is normal in FNH — and this differentiates FNH from HCC. (Book p254)

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman on no medication has an asymptomatic 4 cm liver lesion with a central stellate scar and a normal AFP. The correct management is:
opts: Resection because of the cancer risk
questions.exp: This is FNH: observation is the recommended management. (Book p254)

questions.q: Hepatic adenoma is described as a benign tumour with what risk of cancer?
questions.exp: Hepatic adenoma: benign tumor with a 10% risk of cancer. (Book p254)

questions.q: The strongest association of hepatic adenoma is with:
questions.exp: Strongest association with oral contraceptive pills (OCPs). (Book p254)

questions.q: Unlike FNH, a hepatic adenoma is usually:
questions.exp: Usually symptomatic: hepatomegaly (+). (Book p254)

questions.q: Spontaneous rupture of a hepatic adenoma causes haemoperitoneum, which is the most common:
questions.exp: Spontaneous rupture → haemoperitoneum (m/c non-traumatic cause). (Book p254)

questions.q: On triple phase CT, fat within an adenoma makes the lesion:
questions.exp: Fat content → hypodense. (Book p255)

questions.q: Intratumoral haemorrhage within an adenoma appears:
opts: As a fluid level only on MRI
questions.exp: Intratumoral hemorrhage → hyperdense. (Book p255)

questions.q: On histopathology an adenoma shows sheets of hepatocytes with:
opts: No bile duct structures and no Kupffer cells
Atypical bile duct structures and Kupffer cells
questions.exp: HPE: sheets of hepatocytes, no bile duct structures and no Kupffer cells. (Book p255)

questions.q: The absence of Kupffer cells in an adenoma means it shows:
opts: No 'hot-spot' on a technetium/sulphur colloid scan
A 'hot-spot' on a sulphur colloid scan
questions.exp: No Kupffer cells → no 'hot-spot' on a technetium/sulphur colloid scan — the opposite of FNH. (Book p255)

questions.q: According to this chapter, a hepatic adenoma larger than 5 cm is managed by:
questions.exp: The chapter states: >5 cm — close observation. (Book p255)

questions.q: According to this chapter, a hepatic adenoma smaller than 5 cm is managed by:
opts: Resection because of the risk of HCC
questions.exp: The chapter states: <5 cm — resection (d/t risk of HCC). (Book p255)

questions.q: Which subtype of hepatic adenoma carries the maximum risk of bleeding?
questions.exp: Inflammatory adenoma: maximum risk of bleeding. (Book p255)

questions.q: The HNF-1 alpha mutated adenoma is typically seen in:
opts: Young patients, often with multiple lesions
questions.exp: HNF-1 alpha mutated: young patient, multiple lesions. (Book p255)

questions.q: Which subtype of hepatic adenoma carries the maximum risk of cancer?
questions.exp: β-catenin mutated: maximum risk of cancer. (Book p255)

questions.q: Anabolic steroid associated adenomas and exon-3 mutations are additional features of the:
questions.exp: The Bordeaux list adds that β-catenin mutated adenomas are seen in patients on anabolic steroids and show an exon-3 mutation. (Book p255)

questions.q: The most important risk factor for HCC, ranked above the others in this chapter, is:
questions.exp: Risk factors are listed beginning HBV > HCV. (Book p255)

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a risk factor for HCC?
questions.exp: Risk factors listed: HBV > HCV, alcohol, obesity (NAFLD), Thorotrast exposure, aflatoxin and diabetes mellitus. (Book p255)

questions.q: Thorotrast exposure increases the risk of all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Thorotrast exposure (an old contrast medium) increases the risk of HCC, cholangiocarcinoma and renal cell carcinoma. (Book p255)

questions.q: Thorotrast, listed as a risk factor for HCC, was:
questions.exp: Thorotrast exposure (contrast medium) is listed among the risk factors. (Book p255)

questions.sec: Paraneoplastic Syndromes and Diagnosis of HCC
questions.q: A paraneoplastic syndrome is defined as a syndrome:
opts: Not explained by direct spread or metastasis
Caused by direct invasion of a neighbouring organ
Caused only by the mass effect of the tumour
questions.exp: Paraneoplastic syndrome: a syndrome not explained by direct spread or metastasis. (Book p256)

questions.sec: Paraneoplastic Syndromes and Diagnosis of HCC
questions.q: The most common paraneoplastic syndrome associated with HCC is:
questions.exp: Hypoglycaemia is the m/c paraneoplastic syndrome of HCC. (Book p256)

questions.sec: Paraneoplastic Syndromes and Diagnosis of HCC
questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a paraneoplastic syndrome of HCC?
questions.exp: The listed paraneoplastic syndromes are hypoglycaemia (m/c), Cushing's syndrome and gynaecomastia. (Book p256)

questions.sec: Paraneoplastic Syndromes and Diagnosis of HCC
questions.q: On triple phase CT, HCC in the non-contrast phase is:
questions.exp: CT phases: HCC — non-contrast hypodense, arterial hyperdense, venous early washout. (Book p256)

questions.sec: Paraneoplastic Syndromes and Diagnosis of HCC
questions.q: On triple phase CT, HCC in the arterial phase is:
questions.exp: Arterial phase: hyperdense — the tumour is supplied by the hepatic artery. (Book p256)

questions.sec: Paraneoplastic Syndromes and Diagnosis of HCC
questions.q: The venous phase behaviour that characterises HCC is:
questions.exp: Venous phase: early washout — the hallmark that separates HCC from other lesions. (Book p256)

questions.sec: Paraneoplastic Syndromes and Diagnosis of HCC
questions.q: Metastases in the liver on triple phase CT are:
questions.exp: Metastasis is listed as hypodense, in contrast to the arterial hyperdensity and early washout of HCC. (Book p256)

questions.sec: Paraneoplastic Syndromes and Diagnosis of HCC
questions.q: The CT finding in HCC is described as:
questions.exp: CT finding is classical and diagnostic, and the triple phase CT helps differentiate HCC from metastasis. (Book p256)

questions.sec: Paraneoplastic Syndromes and Diagnosis of HCC
questions.q: The scores listed for assessing liver function in a patient with HCC include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Scores for assessing liver function: Child-Turcotte-Pugh, MELD and PELD. LI-RADS is the imaging scoring system. (Book p256)

questions.q: PIVKA, listed as a tumour marker in HCC, expands to:
opts: Protein induced in vitamin K antagonism (abnormal prothrombin)
Plasma inhibitor of vitamin K absorption
Proliferative index of vitamin K activity
questions.exp: The marker is described as protein induced in vitamin K antagonism (PIVKA), i.e. abnormal prothrombin. (Book p256)

questions.q: Which tumour marker is specifically noted to be raised in the fibrolamellar variant of HCC?
questions.exp: Neurotensin B is raised in the fibrolamellar variant. (Book p256)

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a tumour marker for HCC?
questions.exp: Tumour markers listed: AFP, PIVKA (prothrombin), glypican, HepPar-1 and neurotensin B. (Book p256)

questions.q: Curative resection for HCC is offered to patients with:
opts: Child-Pugh A and an adequate future liver remnant
Child-Pugh B disease with an adequate remnant
Any Child class if the tumour is small
questions.exp: The localized branch: Child-Pugh A with adequate FLR (>25%) goes to resection. (Book p257)

questions.q: A patient with Child-Pugh B or C disease, or an inadequate future liver remnant, is considered for:
questions.exp: Child-Pugh B/C and inadequate FLR (<25%) make the patient a candidate for transplant. (Book p257)

questions.q: FLR expands to:
questions.exp: FLR: functional liver reserve. (Book p257)

questions.q: The future liver remnant is assessed using:
questions.exp: FLR is assessed using Fibroscan. (Book p257)

questions.q: Resection can be done when the future liver remnant is:
questions.exp: >25% — resection can be done. (Book p257)

questions.q: Which procedure is listed for triggering hypertrophy of the other lobe before resection?
questions.exp: Portal vein embolisation triggers hypertrophy of the other lobe. (Book p257)

questions.q: The Nimura technique / ALPPS is listed in the management of HCC under:
opts: Measures used when the future liver remnant is inadequate
questions.exp: Nimura technique/ALPPS appears in the branch dealing with an inadequate FLR. (Book p257)

questions.sec: Milan Criteria, Ablation and Palliative Therapy
questions.q: The Milan criteria for liver transplantation in HCC are:
opts: A single tumour <5 cm or up to 3 tumours each <3 cm, with no metastasis
Any number of tumours provided each is <5 cm
questions.exp: Milan criteria: single tumor <5 cm OR 1-3 tumors <3 cm, with no metastasis. (Book p257)

questions.sec: Milan Criteria, Ablation and Palliative Therapy
questions.q: Radiofrequency ablation is listed for HCC lesions of size:
questions.exp: RFA: <3 cm. (Book p257)

questions.sec: Milan Criteria, Ablation and Palliative Therapy
questions.q: Microwave ablation is listed for lesions:
questions.exp: Microwave ablation: >3 cm. (Book p257)

questions.sec: Milan Criteria, Ablation and Palliative Therapy
questions.q: Which of the following is listed among the local ablative/trans-arterial options when transplantation is not possible?
questions.exp: The listed options are RFA, microwave ablation, percutaneous ethanol injection, TACE and TARE. (Book p257)

questions.sec: Milan Criteria, Ablation and Palliative Therapy
questions.q: Trans-arterial radioembolisation (TARE) uses:
questions.exp: Trans-arterial radioembolisation/TARE — yttrium spheres are used. (Book p257)

questions.sec: Milan Criteria, Ablation and Palliative Therapy
questions.q: Trans-arterial chemoembolisation is abbreviated as:
questions.exp: Trans-arterial chemoembolisation = TACE. (Book p257)

questions.sec: Milan Criteria, Ablation and Palliative Therapy
questions.q: The first-line systemic agent listed for advanced/metastatic HCC is:
questions.exp: Palliative treatment for advanced/metastatic disease: sorafenib (tyrosine kinase inhibitor). (Book p257)

questions.sec: Milan Criteria, Ablation and Palliative Therapy
questions.q: Which immunotherapy drugs are listed for advanced HCC?
questions.exp: The second palliative option listed is pembrolizumab/nivolumab. (Book p257)

questions.sec: Prognostic Indicators and the Fibrolamellar Variant
questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a prognostic indicator for HCC?
questions.exp: Prognostic indicators listed: CLIP, Okuda and BCLC. (Book p257)

questions.sec: Prognostic Indicators and the Fibrolamellar Variant
questions.q: The most common prognostic factor in HCC is:
questions.exp: m/c prognostic factor in HCC: stage of disease. (Book p257)

questions.sec: Prognostic Indicators and the Fibrolamellar Variant
questions.q: The most common site of metastasis from HCC is the:
questions.exp: m/c site of metastasis: lungs. (Book p257)

questions.sec: Prognostic Indicators and the Fibrolamellar Variant
questions.q: The fibrolamellar variant of HCC occurs in:
opts: Young patients with a non-cirrhotic liver
Only in patients with hepatitis B
questions.exp: Fibrolamellar variant: young patients, non-cirrhotic liver, male = female. (Book p257)

questions.sec: Prognostic Indicators and the Fibrolamellar Variant
questions.q: The prognosis of the fibrolamellar variant is:
questions.exp: Fibrolamellar variant: good prognosis. (Book p257)

questions.sec: Prognostic Indicators and the Fibrolamellar Variant
questions.q: In the fibrolamellar variant of HCC the AFP is:
questions.exp: AFP is not raised in the fibrolamellar variant (neurotensin B is the marker that rises). (Book p257)

questions.q: The principles of liver resection listed include:
opts: Reverse Trendelenburg position with aggressive fluid loading
questions.exp: Principle of liver resection: Trendelenburg position + fluid restriction (to keep venous pressure low). (Book p258)

questions.q: The three most critical factors in liver resection are:
opts: Amount of liver resected, blood loss and the condition of the liver (Child-Pugh score)
Portal pressure, bile duct diameter and platelet count
Anaesthesia time, incision length and drain use
questions.exp: The 3 most critical factors: amount of liver resected, blood loss and condition (Child-Pugh score). (Book p258)

questions.q: A future liver remnant of more than 50% is associated with:
questions.exp: FLR >50%: less mortality. (Book p258)

questions.q: Mortality rises when the future liver remnant falls below:
questions.exp: FLR <20-25%: ↑ mortality. (Book p258)

questions.q: All of the following are listed complications of liver resection EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Complications listed: hepatic dysfunction, bile leak, ascites and infections. (Book p258)

questions.q: The most common site of metastasis from colorectal cancer is the:
questions.exp: Liver is the m/c site for colorectal cancer metastases. (Book p258)

questions.q: Approximately what proportion of colorectal cancers show liver metastases?
questions.exp: 60% of colorectal cancers show liver metastases. (Book p258)

questions.q: Liver metastases detected less than 1 year after the primary are termed:
questions.exp: Types: synchronous (<1 yr) and metachronous (>1 yr). (Book p258)

questions.q: Metastases detected more than 1 year after treatment of the primary are:
questions.exp: Metachronous: >1 year. (Book p258)

questions.q: The investigation of choice for colorectal liver metastases shows:
opts: Hypodense lesions on triple phase CT
Hyperdense lesions on triple phase CT
Hot spots on a sulphur colloid scan
questions.exp: Investigation: triple phase CT (IOC) → hypodense lesions. (Book p258)

questions.q: Bevacizumab, used in colorectal liver metastases, is a monoclonal antibody against:
questions.exp: Immunotherapy: bevacizumab — a monoclonal antibody against VEGF. (Book p258)

questions.q: Surgical resection of colorectal liver metastases is advised when:
opts: The future liver remnant is adequate and resection is possible, as it improves survival
There are more than ten lesions
There is extrahepatic disease even if resection is possible
The primary tumour is still in situ
questions.exp: Surgical resection is done if adequate FLR plus resection is possible — and it increases survival. (Book p258)

questions.q: Hepatoblastoma typically presents at what age?
questions.exp: Hepatoblastoma: <3 yrs of age. (Book p259)

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a clinical feature of hepatoblastoma?
opts: Lung metastasis at diagnosis in about 50%
questions.exp: Clinical features: <3 yrs, hepatomegaly, anaemia, lung metastasis at diagnosis (50%) and jaundice — jaundice is a LATE sign. (Book p259)

questions.q: At diagnosis, roughly what proportion of hepatoblastoma patients have lung metastases?
questions.exp: Lung metastasis at diagnosis: 50%. (Book p259)

questions.q: The investigation of choice for hepatoblastoma is:
questions.exp: IOC: triple phase CT (CECT). (Book p259)

questions.q: The sequence of treatment in hepatoblastoma is:
questions.exp: Management: surgery → chemotherapy. (Book p259)

questions.q: The correct statement about hepatoblastoma with metastases is that:
opts: Aggressive treatment is given even if metastases are present
Treatment is palliative only once metastases appear
Only the lung lesion is treated
questions.exp: The page emphasises aggressive treatment even if metastasis is present. (Book p259)

questions.q: The incidence of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is about:
questions.exp: Incidence: 10%. (Book p259)

questions.q: Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is the:
opts: Second most common primary hepatic neoplasm
Third most common primary hepatic neoplasm
questions.exp: It is the 2nd m/c primary hepatic neoplasm (after HCC). (Book p259)

questions.q: Which of the following is a risk factor for intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma?
questions.exp: Risk factors: primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), hepatolithiasis and choledochal cyst. (Book p259)

questions.q: Which risk factor is shared by intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder disease through stone formation within the ducts?
questions.exp: Hepatolithiasis is listed as a risk factor for intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. (Book p259)

questions.q: Compared with HCC, jaundice in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma appears:
questions.exp: Clinical features: jaundice (early sign) and hepatomegaly. (Book p259)

questions.q: The tumour marker picture in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is:
opts: Normal AFP with a markedly raised CA 19-9
Raised AFP with a normal CA 19-9
questions.exp: Investigation: IOC triple phase CT, AFP normal and S. CA 19-9 ↑↑. (Book p259)

questions.q: A 60-year-old with primary sclerosing cholangitis develops a hepatic mass with early jaundice, a normal AFP and a markedly raised CA 19-9. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: PSC is a risk factor, jaundice is early, AFP is normal and CA 19-9 is markedly raised — intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. (Book p259)

units.title: LI-RADS and the Common Liver Tumours
units.sec: LI-RADS and the Common Liver Tumours · p253
units.guide: Triple phase CT is the entry ticket to every liver mass, and LI-RADS turns its appearance into a shared language: LR-1 is certainly benign, LR-5 is certainly HCC, and LR-3 in the middle is where follow-up or biopsy earns its keep.

units.title: Liver Haemangioma
units.guide: Haemangiomas are simply a tangle of vessels, common in women and found by accident. Non-contrast hypodense with peripheral nodular arterial enhancement is the signature; leave them alone unless they are big enough to bleed, hurt or consume clotting factors.

units.title: Focal Nodular Hyperplasia
units.guide: FNH is the great mimicker that needs no operation: a young woman, a central stellate scar fed by a dilated arteriole, bile ductules and Kupffer cells that light up the sulphur colloid scan, and a completely normal AFP. Observe it.

units.title: Hepatic Adenoma
units.guide: Adenoma is FNH's dangerous twin — OCP-related, symptomatic, and the commonest non-traumatic cause of haemoperitoneum when it ruptures. Fat and haemorrhage shape its CT appearance, and the absence of Kupffer cells means a cold sulphur colloid scan.

units.title: Bordeaux Classification of Hepatic Adenoma
units.sec: Bordeaux Classification of Hepatic Adenoma · p255
units.guide: The Bordeaux classification decides an adenoma's behaviour: inflammatory tumours bleed most, HNF-1α tumours present young and multiple, and β-catenin tumours — the anabolic-steroid, exon-3 mutated group — carry the malignant risk.

units.title: Hepatocellular Carcinoma: Risk Factors
units.guide: HCC follows its risk factors: HBV above HCV, then alcohol, NAFLD, aflatoxin and diabetes. Thorotrast is the historical curiosity worth remembering because it also predisposes to cholangiocarcinoma and renal cell carcinoma.

units.title: Paraneoplastic Syndromes and Diagnosis of HCC
units.sec: Paraneoplastic Syndromes and Diagnosis of HCC · p256
units.guide: HCC declares itself on the phases — hypodense, then hyperdense, then early washout — and declares itself systemically through hypoglycaemia, Cushing's syndrome or gynaecomastia, none of which needs a metastasis to explain it.

units.title: Tumour Markers in HCC
units.guide: Markers matter when the scan is equivocal: AFP, PIVKA (the abnormal prothrombin induced by vitamin K antagonism), glypican and HepPar-1 — and neurotensin B, which rises specifically in the fibrolamellar variant.

units.title: Treatment of Localised HCC
units.guide: Resection is a question of reserve rather than courage: Child-Pugh A with an FLR above 25% measured on Fibroscan goes to theatre, and when the remnant is short you can make it grow with portal vein embolisation or an ALPPS-type strategy.

units.title: Milan Criteria, Ablation and Palliative Therapy
units.sec: Milan Criteria, Ablation and Palliative Therapy · p257
units.guide: For everyone else there is a ladder: transplant within Milan criteria, and when no donor appears, RFA under 3 cm, microwave over 3 cm, ethanol injection, TACE or TARE with yttrium spheres — and sorafenib or pembrolizumab/nivolumab once the disease is advanced.

units.title: Prognostic Indicators and the Fibrolamellar Variant
units.sec: Prognostic Indicators and the Fibrolamellar Variant · p257
units.guide: Prognosis is still driven by stage, scored variously by CLIP, Okuda or BCLC, and the lung is where HCC most often lands. The fibrolamellar variant is the welcome exception: a young patient, a non-cirrhotic liver, a normal AFP and a genuinely good outlook.

units.title: Principles of Liver Resection
units.guide: Cutting liver is as much physiology as anatomy: head down, fluids restricted, and three things watched — how much liver is taken, how much blood is lost and how good the liver was to begin with. Below a 20-25% remnant, mortality climbs.

units.title: Colorectal Liver Metastases
units.guide: The liver is where colorectal cancer goes, and it goes there in about 60% of patients. Synchronous lesions within a year and metachronous ones after it are both worth resecting when the remnant allows, usually alongside bevacizumab against VEGF.

units.title: Hepatoblastoma
units.guide: Hepatoblastoma is the tumour of the under-threes: hepatomegaly, anaemia, half of them already seeded to lung at diagnosis and jaundice only late. Even with metastases the page insists on aggressive surgery followed by chemotherapy.

units.title: Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma
units.guide: Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma closes the chapter as the second commonest primary liver cancer, born of PSC, stones or a choledochal cyst. Unlike HCC it jaundices early, keeps AFP normal and sends CA 19-9 soaring.
